name: What AI Does Well
title: What AI Does Well
answer: This idea says AI is most useful for repetitive, heavy with language, and easy to check work, such as parent letters or lunch counts. It matters because the strongest school results in the book come when AI helps a skilled adult rather than replacing one, and because every AI output still needs a human check. The book pairs each AI strength with the part of the work a person still does.

crumbs.name: What AI Can and Cannot Do

sections.body: The idea is that AI has a recognizable set of strengths, and the book lists six that appear most often in this Volume. Those strengths fit work that repeats, involves a lot of language, and can be checked by a person. In a school, that covers more of the day than people might expect, from parent letters to lunch counts. The problem it solves is not a shortage of software but a shortage of time and attention for routine language work. The book's answer is to let AI carry that work while a person keeps the checking and the judgment.
sections.heading: The idea

sections.body: In practice, the book shows AI supporting adults rather than running the lesson on its own. In a Southern US school district, 900 new tutors worked with 1,800 students, and an AI assistant suggested what the tutor might say next, talking to the tutor and not the student. In Nigeria, students aged about 15 worked in pairs with an AI chat tool in after school sessions over six weeks. Teachers opened each session with a prompt that told the AI to act as a tutor, not an answer machine, and they walked the room the whole time. The text gives no other grade bands, but the pattern in both cases is an adult designing the AI use and staying present while it happens.
sections.heading: How it works in school

sections.body: The book does not attach a formal evidence label to this idea, but it reports two studies. In the Southern US district, students whose tutors had the AI assistant were 4 percentage points more likely to master a topic, and students of tutors who actually used it gained 14 points. The tool cost about $20 per tutor per year, and it did not raise end of year state test scores, which the book says is a reminder that short gains do not always last (Wang et al., 2024). In Nigeria, students gained 0.31 standard deviations, one of the larger effects measured for a program that short (De Simone et al., 2025). The book also notes that Figure 1.3 lists the six strengths that show up most often in this Volume.
sections.heading: What the evidence says

sections.body: The limits are clear in the text: none of the AI strengths is finished until someone checks it, and the best results come when AI supports a skilled adult instead of replacing one. The tutors, not the software, did the teaching. Short gains do not always last, as the Southern US district's end of year state test scores show. Neither success came from turning students loose with a chatbot, so adults must design how the AI is used and stay in the room while it is. The decisions about what to check, how to prompt the AI, and when to keep teaching in person stay with a person.
